items.title: Hooks: let a hook prove which thread it belongs to (OS-verifiable per-thread identity for local services)

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: hooks
labels.description: Issues related to event hooks

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI (`codex` 0.162.1, macOS, app-server daemon enabled — `feature.daemon_auto_start=true`), with lifecycle hooks (`[features] hooks = true`, `~/.codex/hooks.json`).

### What feature would you like to see?

**A way for a hook (or any process a Codex session spawns) to prove to a local, same-user service which Codex thread it belongs to — something the OS or Codex itself can vouch for, not a value the process merely claims.**

Context: [Gyredeck](https://github.com/j-kizt/gyredeck-macos) is a local menu-bar companion that gives each agent session (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity) a private mailbox and shared "sync rooms". Today every hook identifies its session by sending the session id in a request (`?as=<id>`), and since every hook on a machine runs as the same Unix user, nothing stops one process from naming another session's id and reading its mail. The planned fix is a native broker: a Unix socket whose listener asks the kernel who connected (`LOCAL_PEERTOKEN` → pid/pidversion), resolves that process's parent with `proc_pidinfo`, and binds **that parent** to the session id the hook names. The hook then never names a mailbox; the broker chooses it.

That works for Claude Code, whose hooks are children of the per-session `claude` process. It cannot work for Codex as of 0.162.1, measured on a live machine:

- Hooks are spawned by the **shared app-server daemon** (one process serving every thread), so the hook's parent identifies "Codex", not a thread. The TUI process is not an ancestor of the hook at all (TUI → shell; app-server daemon → daemon supervisor → launchd).
- The same daemon also runs the agent's own tool commands, so a listener cannot even distinguish "a hook" from "a command the agent ran".
- The hook payloads (`SessionStart`, `UserPromptSubmit`, … per `codex-rs/hooks/src/schema.rs`) carry session/turn ids, transcript path, cwd and model, and the launcher (`codex-rs/hooks/src/engine/command_runner.rs`) rebuilds the environment from the session snapshot — none of it is OS-verifiable. A pid or thread id placed in the payload or environment would still be a claim.

Any of these would close it; the first is the smallest:

1. **A per-thread capability token** minted by the daemon for each hook run (and ideally each tool process), passed to the hook, and **verifiable by a local service through the app-server API** (e.g. `thread/verifyHookToken` → `{ thread_id, turn_id, expires }`). The service never trusts the hook; it asks Codex.
2. A per-thread Unix socket or file descriptor handed to the hook, so the peer credential on *that* socket is the thread's, not the daemon's.
3. An app-server request that answers "which thread does pid *N* (a process Codex spawned) belong to", checked against Codex's own records of what it spawned and when.

### Additional information

Measured with `~/.codex/logs_2.sqlite` and the live process tree on macOS 15 (Darwin 25.6): every hook and tool process under one Codex session had parent pid 41451 (`app-server-daemon/releases/0.162.1-aarch64-apple-darwin/bin/codex`), while the TUI was pid 54715 under a shell. Reviewed against the `rust-v0.162.1` sources named above. Happy to test a build or a proposed API — the Gyredeck side is in progress at j-kizt/gyredeck-macos#119 and will treat Codex sessions as "unsupported, fall back" until Codex can vouch for them.

I'm a paying ChatGPT Pro user who uses Codex for complex, multi-step software development, architecture reviews, and code audits.

Please prioritize:

Especially during the 28-day improvement initiative, I hope the team will treat meaningful *user productivity* as the bar for improvements—not just interface conveniences or raw response speed.

items.body: ### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)? 26.1007.21159 ### What subscription do you have? Plus ### What platform is your computer? Darwin 24.6.0 x86_64 i386 ### What issue are you seeing? ChatGPT Work cloud chats started in the macOS desktop app cannot create a simple text file on my Desktop, even with **Full Access** selected in the composer and Desktop access already allowed in macOS. The run-location description for **In the cloud** says: “Available on any device and can access your computer.” The Full access description says: “Unrestricted access to the internet and any file on your computer.” However, the affected agent reports receiving a restricted execution configuration that excludes Desktop writes. The same basic Desktop file-creation task works in Work local chats using **On your computer**. Cloud chats used to be able to do this for me; I do not know the exact date this stopped working. The strongest discrepancy is between the Full Access selection and the affected agent’s reported `workspace-write` / `restricted` execution settings. The Desktop write failed and no file was created. ### What steps can reproduce the bug? 1. Open the ChatGPT macOS desktop app and keep it running and connected. 2. Start a new Work chat and choose **In the cloud**. 3. Select **Full Access** in the composer permissions menu. Desktop access is already allowed for the app in macOS. 4. Send this request: > Go into my desktop and create a .txt file that simply says "Testing, testing, 123 – dubstep is cool." 5. The assistant attempts to create `~/Desktop/dubstep-test.txt`, reports “operation not permitted,” and reports that its follow-up check found no file. **Comparison:** Start a Work chat using **On your computer** and request a text file on Desktop. Local Work can complete the task on the same Mac. ### What is the expected behavior? With Full Access selected, macOS Desktop access granted, and the Mac connected, Work cloud chats should be able to create the requested file on Desktop, as local Work chats can. If another policy or limitation prevents that access, the app should clearly explain it and reflect the effective restriction in the permissions UI. Selecting Full Access should not silently result in a restricted write configuration that excludes Desktop. ### Additional information ### Environment - Application: ChatGPT desktop app for macOS - App version: **26.1007.21159** - App build: **20052** - Operating system: **macOS Sequoia 15.7.9** - macOS build: **24G830** - Architecture: **Intel / x86_64** - Subscription: **ChatGPT Plus** - Affected mode: **Work → In the cloud**, with the chat started in the desktop app - Permission selection for the failed test: **Full Access** - Working comparison: **Work → On your computer** - Report date: **October 9, 2026** The installed app version/build, macOS version/build, and architecture were checked directly on this Mac. ### Feedback ID I submitted feedback using `/feedback` **from the affected “Create Desktop File Test” Work cloud chat**: ```text 89b593cc-d97f-4e8c-9f6c-cae828ffa601 ``` ### Failed test and reported execution permissions In the affected conversation, **Create Desktop File Test**, the assistant reported: - The Desktop directory existed and its metadata was accessible. This alone does not establish that files inside it were readable. - The attempt to create `dubstep-test.txt` failed with exit code `1`: ```text zsh:1: operation not permitted: /Users//Desktop/dubstep-test.txt ``` - A subsequent check returned `No such file or directory`; no file was created. The username in the error above has been redacted for this public report. The agent described its supplied execution permissions as follows: | Reported execution setting | Value | | --- | --- | | Filesystem sandbox mode | `workspace-write` | | Filesystem permission profile | `restricted` | | Writable locations | Chat workspace, temporary directories, and certain tool directories | | Desktop included as writable | No | | Requests for elevated sandbox access | Configured to be automatically rejected | The agent did not submit an elevation request. The actual file write was denied; this was not a case of me rejecting an approval prompt. These execution settings and test results are reported by the affected agent. They are not an independently captured runtime configuration dump. The failure is consistent with a permission mismatch, but the error alone does not identify which enforcement layer denied the write. ### Configuration checks and UI context A separate local Work diagnostic found Full Access saved in the app’s current permission settings and no explicit file-access restriction in the local configuration or standard managed-policy locations it checked. An earlier affected cloud chat could also read actual app configuration files on the Mac but failed to create a Desktop file. This suggests that local computer access is available at least for some operations, while the selected write permissions are not being applied as expected. The precise cause is unconfirmed. The **Ask for approval** option is greyed out in cloud Work. Inspection of the installed app’s bundled code found an explicit cloud-mode condition disabling that option and a tooltip reading “Unavailable while working in the cloud.” I am including this as UI context, not claiming that the disabled option causes the write failure. ### Pictures Here are my Work settings under settings > configuration (in the desktop app): Here is a screenshot showing the “Ask for approval” permission greyed out when composing a new Work cloud chat: Apparently my agent said that this being greyed out is intention according to the app’s code. The agent did not find any official documentation to support this, though.

## Summary

During an authorized, long-running **ChatGPT Work** task on Windows, the **Highwatch Builder** worker stopped work on a set of Arkenforge encounter maps. It said it was **declining to run a previously working custom-control helper** because the governing instructions for that session prohibited the method. It simultaneously acknowledged that the user **had already authorized the work**, that no further permission was needed, and that **no map editing was running**. The visible goal status was **"Goal stalled"**.

When the user attempted to recover by moving/branching the conversation, they separately reported that **the worker conversation would not branch**. The screenshots provided so far document the stalled worker and its suggested handoff; they **do not establish the specific error code, exact branching UI operation, or backend reason that branching failed**.

The report is about **recoverability, clear explanation of a real control limitation, context-preserving continuation, and branch/fork reliability**. It does **not** request that any prohibited helper be executed or that session restrictions be bypassed.

## Environment and evidence scope

- Product/surface: ChatGPT **Work**, Windows desktop UI (not a verified Codex CLI reproduction).
- Visible task: **Highwatch Builder** / an October 10 Arkenforge encounter-map assignment.
- Model displayed in an accompanying screenshot: **GPT-6 Astra Ultra**. The actual served backend and effective permissions are not independently verified.
- UI displayed **Full access**, but the worker stated the currently available connection could not perform the requested Arkenforge desktop operations. A UI label alone does not prove tool availability or authorize bypassing restrictions.
- The goal banner displayed approximately **"Goal stalled"** after about **1h 9m**; this is a UI observation, not a measured execution trace.
- Specific app/package build, task/thread IDs, fork error string and diagnostics: **not yet captured or verified**.
- User screenshots of the messages, goal status and navigation are available; this public post quotes key text but does not contain the original image attachments or private local project/control scripts.

## Observed sequence (Oct. 10, 2026)

1. The ongoing task was to prepare/verify **fourteen existing encounter maps** for Arkenforge, with seven player characters and encounter testing. It involved controlling Arkenforge on the **Tickwood** machine/project.
2. The worker acknowledged previously providing contradictory blockers and said: **"No map editing is currently running."**
3. Asked **"so you are refusing to work?"**, the worker stated:  
   > "I am declining to run the old custom-control helper because the instructions governing this session prohibit that method."

   It continued:
   > "That leaves me unable to perform your requested Arkenforge desktop work on Tickwood with the current connection. You have already authorized the work; I am not waiting for more permission from you. The practical result is that your work is stalled. I won't pretend otherwise."
4. The user asked whether they needed another chat because the worker was not continuing. The worker answered that a new chat might not have different control capabilities and it did not want to send the user into another setup loop.
5. It claimed a saved handoff existed, linked as **"Current project state and remaining work"**, **"Previously working Tickwood control wrapper"**, and **"Completed fourteen-map verification record"**.
6. In a later response, it claimed the **fourteen maps with seven player characters** had been saved/reopened, the **encounter-piece test map** was prepared but **hide/reveal behavior still required testing**, and the saved checkpoint and scripts remained available. **These are worker statements, not independently verified preservation or successful handoff.**
7. Separately, the user reported that **branching the worker conversation did not work**, so creating a continuity-preserving branch was not an effective recovery route. A navigation screenshot also shows a **"Worktree init failed"** entry elsewhere in the workspace; its relationship to this Highwatch task is **not established** and must not be treated as the branch failure's cause.

## Expected behavior

- If an earlier helper or interaction method is prohibited, identify the **real supported restriction and current tool capability**, without pretending work is progressing or inventing new approval requirements.
- Offer a **permitted** means to regain desktop control, continue allowable subtasks, or recover/transfer the task to an authorized environment without forcing the user to reconstruct the fourteen-map context.
- Explicitly distinguish **saved artifacts**, **worker-asserted state**, **verified application state**, **remaining tests**, and **unavailable operations**.
- Allow a user to branch/fork an existing Work conversation when supported, or provide an **actionable, diagnostic error** when not supported. Preserve access to the previous transcript, references and handoff information.
- A stalled goal should identify a specific blocker and actionable next step rather than leaving the user stuck after substantial task time.

## Actual behavior / impact

- User-authorized work stopped; the worker expressly declined the prior control route and reported no compatible desktop control through the current connection.
- No map editing or pending hide/reveal tests were completed in the cited messages.
- The user reports **branch/fork unavailable**, limiting recovery from an unusable task.
- The user faces repeated setup, lost time, and uncertainty over which portions of the worker's claimed completed state are independently verified.

## Engineering investigation requested

1. In this Work session, **what exact tool/permission/session restriction** prohibited the old control helper? Was the tool previously available to this task, and did capability or session policy change during execution?
2. Was a **supported Arkenforge desktop-control path** present? If not, why was the limitation surfaced only after a prolonged task, and what specific authorized recovery path should the UI offer?
3. Can the task's alleged **saved checkpoint and fourteen-map state** be restored/inspected in a new permitted session **without recreating user instructions or losing prior work**?
4. For the reported **branching failure**, did the UI disable branch, reject it, fail during creation, or fail to open a new branch? Please check the relevant server/client logs and expose an error code or reason to the user. Specific reproduction/error information can be provided privately if needed.
5. Clarify how **"Full access"**, actual computer-use availability, **"Goal stalled"**, and the worker's claimed handoff should be represented so they cannot create misleading expectations.

## Related but not assumed duplicates

- **#52665** — Earlier Tickwood Work task involving premature completion reports, disputed approval gating, and repeated compaction. This report concerns **desktop-control availability and branch recovery in a separate map-building task**, not the same observed failure.
- **#52340** — Other user's project-chat branching failure with a specific thread-store error. **Potentially relevant only**; the same error has **not** been observed here.

Please treat the branch/fork symptom and the desktop-control restriction as **separately investigable** until evidence establishes a connection. Additional screenshots and account/task identifiers can be supplied through a private authenticated support channel; please do not request private machine access details, credentials or logs in public replies.

### What issue are you seeing?

nghi@Nghis-Mac-mini vvpanel % codex
Error: account/read failed during TUI bootstrap: account/read failed: failed to load workspace requirements (code -32603)

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

**Codex CLI 0.162.1 – TUI Bootstrap Failure After Upgrade (macOS)**

After upgrading Codex CLI to `0.162.1` on macOS, running `codex` fails with:

```text
Error: account/read failed during TUI bootstrap:
account/read failed: failed to load workspace requirements (code -32603)
```

- Authentication is valid (`Logged in using ChatGPT`).
- Logging out and back in does not help.
- File descriptor limit is `1048576`.
- **Workaround:** `codex -c log_dir="$HOME/.codex/log"` works.
- However, setting the exact same `log_dir` in `~/.codex/config.toml` (root level) does not resolve the issue.
- Restarting the app-server daemon reports: `app server is running but is not managed by codex app-server daemon`.

**Expected:** Codex should start normally without CLI overrides.

This issue appeared immediately after upgrading the CLI and may be a regression in the TUI bootstrap or configuration loading process.

### What is the expected behavior?

Codex CLI should start normally when running `codex` after upgrading, without requiring additional CLI flags or workarounds. Configuration values in `~/.codex/config.toml` should behave consistently with equivalent `-c` command-line overrides.

### Additional information

The issue started immediately after upgrading to Codex CLI `0.162.1` on macOS.

Interestingly, passing `-c log_dir="$HOME/.codex/log"` allows Codex to start successfully, but setting the exact same value in `~/.codex/config.toml` (at the root level) does not work.

Authentication is valid, and logging out and back in does not resolve the issue. The file descriptor limit is also sufficiently high (`1048576`).

This suggests a possible regression in configuration loading or TUI bootstrap behavior introduced by the CLI upgrade.

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: connectivity
labels.description: Issues involving networking or endpoint connectivity problems (disconnections)

items.body:
## Description

My existing Dot disappeared entirely from the Windows desktop app’s sidebar. Meanwhile, the same Dot remained accessible and active at https://chatgpt.com/dots/home.

The web UI showed the Dot thinking and its connected computer as ready. This confirms that web access remained available at the time observed; it does not establish that every local task operation was succeeding.

Before the sidebar entry disappeared, the desktop app intermittently showed:

- `Local Work executor registration failed (HTTP 403)`
- “Couldn't load your dot”
- `We couldn’t check access to messages`

The connection temporarily recovered without any configuration change, then failed again. I do not have a deterministic reproduction.

## Environment

- OS: Windows
- Desktop app version: `26.1007.21434`, build `13901`, production channel
- Windows package version: `26.1007.2314.0`
- The app’s update checker reported `up_to_date` when checked.
- Mihomo proxy with TUN enabled at the time of inspection

The problem was noticed after an app update. However, the same executor registration error also appeared in logs from the earlier installed package, so the evidence does **not** establish that the update caused it.

## Observed sequence

1. Local executor registration intermittently failed with HTTP 403.
2. The executor subsequently connected successfully.
3. Dot access recovered temporarily without a configuration change.
4. Desktop Dot loading/message-access errors recurred.
5. The “Your Dot” sidebar entry disappeared entirely.
6. The same Dot remained accessible and active in the web interface.

## Confirmed diagnostic evidence

The following is a sanitized summary of application diagnostics, rather than a verbatim log excerpt.

All timestamps below are **2026-10-10, UTC+08:00**.

| Time | Recorded observation |
|---|---|
| 10:39:16.195 | Local executor startup failed with `Local Work executor registration failed (HTTP 403)`. |
| 11:52:23.987 | Executor rendezvous connection became unavailable with `read_error`; subsequent attempts reported `websocket_error`. |
| 11:52:43.832 | The replacement executor connected to rendezvous. |
| 11:54:49.028 | `/tbo` failed with HTTP 403 and `errorCode=cloudflare_challenge`. |
| 11:55:35.623 | `/tbo/{redacted}/environment/status` failed with HTTP 403 and `cloudflare_challenge`. This establishes a status-fetch failure, not that the executor was offline. |
| From 12:00:01.780 | Message-related requests returned 403, alongside `client.room_fetch` and `client.history_fetch` failures. |
| 12:10:02.434 | `/accounts/check/{version}` failed with HTTP 403 and `cloudflare_challenge`. |

Other affected desktop routes included `/tbo/primary`, `/settings/user`, `/sentinel/heartbeat`, and `/celsius/ws/user`.

A read-only connection inspection correlated the executor’s local socket with an existing Mihomo connection to `codex-cloud-environments.chatgpt.com:443`. The recorded outbound chain used a proxy node, **not DIRECT**.

This verifies the inspected executor connection’s route. It does not establish the route or response source for every earlier failed request.

No server request ID or CF-Ray was available in the relevant failure records inspected.

## What remains unconfirmed

- The exact runtime condition that hid the sidebar entry was not obtainable.
- Static inspection of the installed client suggests that Dot visibility depends on account capability data, including `tbo_available`. However, the actual runtime capability values and branch taken were not captured.
- Therefore, account-check failures causing the sidebar disappearance remain a hypothesis.
- The exact response body and headers for the executor registration 403 were unavailable. Related API requests were classified as Cloudflare challenges, but that does not conclusively classify the registration response itself.

## Expected behavior

An existing Dot should remain discoverable when account-capability or Dot metadata requests temporarily fail. The app should display a recoverable loading/connection error instead of silently removing the entry.

A working executor connection, desktop metadata retrieval, and message access should be reported separately.

## Request for investigation

Please investigate:

1. Whether failed account-capability requests can hide “Your Dot” while the same Dot remains active on the web.
2. How desktop API requests recover from Cloudflare challenges.
3. A supported recovery procedure that preserves running tasks, the existing Dot, and computer authorization.
4. Whether a released desktop build addresses this behavior.

## Related reports

- [#51213](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/51213): Similar sidebar disappearance while background work continues, but with different recorded errors.
- [#50034](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/50034): The same executor registration error and related desktop Cloudflare challenges, reported on macOS.

These reports are related observations, not confirmation of a shared root cause.

我正在使用 Codex 修复自有项目中 VersityGW 的并发上传问题。
任务目标是防止迟到分片重新创建已结束的上传目录，以及旧上传覆盖
后写对象；同时正确处理取消上传和清理失败。

工作仅涉及本地仓库源码与回归测试，没有访问外部攻击目标，
没有执行生产部署、真实设备操作或使用真实云端凭据。

同一个独立开发会话两次被以下错误中断：
“This content was flagged for possible cybersecurity risk.”

3. 当前账户、模型和 Codex 执行入口是否需要额外访问审批？

Uploaded thread: 01a12360-5d82-7d41-b033-3c14bc58fc1f

我希望在修复自有项目中 VersityGW 的并发上传问题时，不再进行重复安全拦截

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1007.11041

### What subscription do you have?

Chatgpt Pro 

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26100.0 x64

### What issue are you seeing?

During a long-running conversation, opening a running subagent from the Subagents sidebar, or switching between concurrently running subagents, can cause the entire Codex UI to reload.

After the reload, the most recent user input in the parent conversation temporarily disappears from the visible transcript. The missing content becomes visible again after approximately **33–47 seconds** of waiting.

Configuration and observed conditions:
   - **Model**: 6.1 Sol
   - **Reasoning effort**: Ultra
   - **Approximate duration of the affected session**: More than 14 hours
   - **Navigation entry point**: Subagents sidebar
   - **Selected subagent status**: Running

When multiple subagents are running, one subagent’s conversation may initially render successfully. Switching to another running subagent can then trigger the same UI reload and temporary disappearance of recent parent-conversation input.

Once the issue starts in the affected session, it can be reproduced repeatedly through subsequent attempts to open or switch between running subagents. Not every initial subagent selection necessarily fails.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

**Precondition**: Use the affected long-running conversation with recent user input in the parent conversation and one or more running subagents. The observed session had been in use for more than 14 hours; a minimum duration or turn-count threshold has not been established.

**Path A — Opening a running subagent**
1. Open the affected parent conversation while subagents are running.
2. Confirm that the latest user input is visible in the parent conversation.
3. Click a subagent marked Running in the Subagents sidebar to inspect its conversation.
4. Observe that the entire Codex UI reloads.
5. After the reload, inspect the parent conversation. Its most recent user input is temporarily missing from the visible transcript.
6. Wait approximately 30 seconds or more. The missing content becomes visible again.

**Path B — Switching between running subagents**

1. In the affected session, have multiple subagents running concurrently.
2. Open running subagent A from the sidebar. Its conversation may render successfully.
3. Select another running subagent, B, in the sidebar.
4. The switch can trigger the same full UI reload.
5. Recent input in the parent conversation becomes temporarily invisible and later reappears, as described above.

After recovery, further attempts to open or switch between running subagents can reproduce the issue again in the affected session.

### What is the expected behavior?

- Clicking a running subagent in the sidebar should correctly render **the selected subagent’s current conversation.**

- Switching between concurrently running subagents should correctly display the newly selected subagent’s conversation without reloading the entire Codex UI.

- The parent conversation’s recent messages should remain available and visible when returning to it.

- Inspecting or switching subagents should not require waiting tens of seconds for parent messages to reappear or resending a message to restore their display.

### Additional information

**Observed recovery behavior**

- **Waiting alone**: The missing parent-conversation content reappears after approximately 33–47 seconds or more.

- **Resending the same message**: Sending the same user message to the parent agent again makes the missing content reappear sooner.

Resending the message is an observed way to accelerate display recovery. Whether the repeated message causes additional task execution has not been established.

**Scope and uncertainties**

- The issue is repeatedly reproducible within the affected session. Reproduction in a fresh session has not been established.

- The session duration of more than 14 hours is an observed condition, not a confirmed trigger threshold.

- Ultra was enabled during the observed failures. Whether other reasoning settings are affected has not been established.

- The visible behavior is a full UI reload. Whether the application process exits or a renderer crashes has not been confirmed.

- The messages eventually reappear in the UI. Whether the parent task continues normally throughout the interruption has not been verified.

**Potentially related issues**

[#32832](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/32832)

[#50020](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/50020)

This report documents opening and switching between **running subagents through the sidebar, a full UI reload, and temporary loss of visible parent-conversation input followed by recovery after 33–47 seconds**.

A shared root cause with the linked reports has not been established.

items.body:
**Subject: URGENT — GPT-6 Astra High Exhausted Nearly Entire Freshly Reset 5-Hour and Weekly Codex Allowances in ~30 Seconds**

**Product:** OpenAI Codex  
**Subscription:** ChatGPT Plus  
**Platform:** macOS / MacBook  
**Model:** GPT-6 Astra  
**Reasoning effort:** High  
**Date:** October 9, 2026  
**Approximate time:** 11:50–11:55 PM EDT (UTC−4)

### Issue Description

I experienced what appears to be a severe Codex usage-accounting or model-execution defect.

Immediately after receiving a fresh usage reset, I initiated a GPT-6 Astra High session in Codex to organize an existing aerospace engineering development project.

**Within approximately 30 seconds, the session depleted nearly my entire freshly reset five-hour allowance AND nearly my entire weekly allowance.**

This occurred during the initialization of a multi-agent coordination workflow, not during a prolonged simulation, computationally intensive engineering analysis, or extended coding session.

The task involved identifying recent relevant Codex conversations, gathering technical handoff summaries, and organizing existing engineering work under a lead agent.

The observed usage depletion was extraordinarily disproportionate to the elapsed time and expected workload.

### Expected Behavior

A short agent-initialization and engineering coordination task should consume usage consistent with actual model execution and documented billing or quota rates.

The task should not unexpectedly exhaust nearly an entire weekly allowance immediately following a reset without a corresponding, explainable amount of computation or token consumption.

### Actual Behavior

1. My five-hour and weekly Codex allowances had just been refreshed.
2. I started a GPT-6 Astra High session on my MacBook.
3. The session began an agent-coordination and conversation-recovery task.
4. Within approximately 30 seconds, nearly both refreshed usage allowances were depleted.
5. This severely disrupted my ability to continue ongoing engineering work across my Codex environments.

### Requested Investigation

Please investigate:

1. The exact token usage and allowance charges associated with this session.
2. Whether subagent spawning, repeated polling, conversation recovery, or tool-call loops caused abnormal usage amplification.
3. Whether cached-context tokens or internal agent operations were incorrectly accounted for.
4. Whether the five-hour and weekly allowances were debited correctly.
5. Whether this behavior matches other reported GPT-6 Astra usage-limit regressions.

A potentially related public report is:

https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/51864

### Requested Resolution

I request a review of the session's usage accounting and a clear explanation of why approximately 30 seconds of activity consumed nearly both refreshed allowances.

**If an accounting or execution defect is confirmed, I request correction of the affected usage balance and restoration of any allowance consumed incorrectly, where technically and administratively possible.**

This incident occurred immediately after a reset and effectively eliminated my available Codex capacity before meaningful engineering work could proceed.

I can provide usage screenshots, the Codex conversation reference, application version, and available execution logs.

Please escalate this to the appropriate Codex engineering or usage-metering team for investigation.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1002.52244 (build 13536), Installed Windows package version: 26.1002.7124.0

### What subscription do you have?

Pro Max

### What platform is your computer?

Windows

### What issue are you seeing?

The dot’s “Last active” timestamp and thinking/activity indicator remain stale in the Windows desktop app, even while messages send and replies arrive normally. I have observed this on multiple Windows machines.
During investigation on October 9, 2026, the stored last-activity timestamp was still October 7 at 19:44 UTC, despite subsequent conversations. Logs showed three successful live-room subscriptions and four successful message sends with corresponding pub/sub receipts, but the activity display remained stale.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

I do not have a reliable sequence that reproduces this from a clean launch. Once it occurs, continuing the conversation does not necessarily refresh the activity display. Messaging itself remains usable. There is no specific user-facing error message.

### What is the expected behavior?

The activity indicator and “Last active” timestamp should reflect current activity and recover after the live connection reconnects.

### Additional information

Read-only inspection suggests that activity updates use a live subscription and activity_status events. Successful subscriptions and message delivery do not prove that fresh activity events reached the UI. The complete event-to-render path has not been captured, so the root cause is still unknown.

items.body:
### Environment
- Codex CLI: 0.162.1
- Codex runs on a remote Linux development machine over SSH.
- Local terminal supports Cmd-click to open URLs in the local browser.

### Reproduction
1. In a normal SSH shell, run `printf 'https://www.google.com\n'`.
2. Cmd-click the URL. The local browser opens successfully.
3. Start Codex in the same SSH terminal and ask it to print https://www.google.com.
4. Cmd-click the URL in Codex's output.

### Actual behavior
Codex displays:
```text
Failed to open browser for https://www.google.com: No valid browsers detected. You can specify one in BROWSER environment variable
```
This suggests the click is handled inside Codex and attempts to launch a browser on the remote machine.

### Expected behavior
Cmd-click should preserve the terminal's native URL handling and open the local browser, as it does outside Codex.

### Additional context
This worked previously in my setup, but I have not identified the last working Codex version. I suspect a regression after an update.
The same error occurs for an OAuth device verification URL, so it is not specific to Google.

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

This incident affected the dot’s own cloud execution environment while I was communicating through ChatGPT on the web. I do not have a verified desktop app or backend execution-service version for the incident.

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro. Exact plan tier can be supplied privately if needed.

### What platform is your computer?

Client: Windows, using ChatGPT in a web browser. Affected execution host: OpenAI-hosted Linux cloud computer belonging to my dot. The affected files and test were not running on my Windows laptop or Mac.

### What issue are you seeing?

Summary
I’m reporting a recurring loss of accessible working state on my dot’s cloud computer. During the latest incident, filesystem operations stalled while an offline software test was running. The execution service subsequently disconnected. When command access returned, recent source worktrees, Git history locations and test evidence were missing, while older project files remained.
Reported filesystem usage fell from roughly 30 GB to 3.3 GB. This includes build caches, binaries and generated test artifacts; it should not be interpreted as 26 GB of unique source code or proof of permanent physical deletion.
I did not click Pause, Reboot, Delete or Reset, or otherwise interact with the cloud environment during the incident. The observations below come from commands run by my assistant and retained conversation/tool results, not OpenAI backend logs.
Environment
- Product: ChatGPT dots, using the dot’s own Linux cloud computer
- Client used for this conversation: Windows web browser
- Workload: offline Rust software development and verification, with separate implementation and review workers
- Working files: task scratch and shared workspace directories
- User’s Windows laptop and Mac were not executing the affected test
- This was not an ordinary temporary data-analysis session or a repository-backed Codex Cloud task
- Exact frontend and execution-service versions were not captured
Observed timeline
All times are UTC on October 10, 2026.
- 02:24:37: An end-to-end offline test started against a pinned source revision. Thirteen focused author tests had passed before this run
- 02:33:43: The last observed database progress recorded allocation of an output copy. The test had already passed several reader-selection, stale/corrupt-source and interrupted-write retry checks
- Around 02:35: Separate workers began encountering stalled filesystem operations, including simple file inspection and directory listing. These were not limited to the product test
- 02:38: A filesystem check still reported approximately 30 GB used, with only about 183 MB available. The current source revision and running-test receipt were still readable
- 02:55:03: The current kernel’s boot time, read after access returned. This does not independently establish the previous kernel’s identity or the exact moment the task was attached to a different environment
- Around 02:58: Attempts to resume existing execution sessions returned: “exec-server transport disconnected; failed to resume exec-server session: recovery timed out after 25s”
- Around 03:01: Commands from a temporary directory worked again. The original top-level working directory existed, but recent implementation worktrees and the latest test receipt were absent. Reported filesystem usage was approximately 3.3 GB
- Subsequent read-only inspection found older pre-code and unrelated files, but not the recent implementation trees, verification directories or runtime test roots previously used by the task
The interrupted test has no observed final exit status. Its result remains unknown and has not been credited as passing.
Evidence of a filesystem or environment transition
1. Changed overlay identity
An environment record recovered from an externally saved, manifest-verified archive identifies an earlier overlay mount. The current mount has a different identifier. This supports a change in the presented filesystem environment; it does not identify whether the mechanism was replacement, restoration, reassociation or another lifecycle operation.
2. Recent metadata timestamps on older files
Several surviving directories have metadata-change timestamps around 03:01 UTC, while retaining older modification timestamps, including October 5 dates. This is consistent with files being restored or rematerialized, but ctime is not a creation timestamp and does not establish the snapshot’s age.
3. Missing state across multiple categories
The disappearance affected source worktrees, Git-history locations, test receipts, build outputs and runtime roots. A stopped test process alone would not explain those missing directories.
4. Low available storage before the incident
The earlier filesystem had approximately 183 MB available. This is relevant diagnostic context. We have not established that disk exhaustion caused the stall or transition, and no captured ENOSPC error establishes that explanation.
5. Diagnostic limits
Kernel logs were inaccessible. Counters read from the current kernel cannot rule out an out-of-memory or other failure in a previous environment. The assistant cannot inspect platform-side lifecycle, storage-association or snapshot logs.
Cleanup actions and scope
The assistant had previously removed explicitly bounded generated metadata and redundant caches. Those recorded removals were far smaller than the observed usage change, excluded original source and verification receipts, and were followed by successful builds, focused tests and the subsequent running test.
These recorded cleanup actions do not explain the broad disappearance of recent source and evidence. However, this report is not an assertion that every platform action or filesystem operation has been audited; that requires backend records.
Earlier incident on the same dot
This is not my first experience of missing work in this conversation. Before the current incident, we had already discussed missing research progress, including what I described as 12–14 research cycles/runs.
That earlier event led me to request backups on my laptop and regular ZIP checkpoints explicitly. My instructions included saving everything so another environment loss would not erase the work, and continuing to send ZIPs periodically.
The earlier incident’s exact onset, filesystem identifiers and complete loss inventory are not established in this report. Please correlate it with the earlier activity in the same dot conversation. I am reporting recurrence of the user-visible problem, not claiming that both incidents have a proven common cause.
Impact and recovery
- Recent source changes and verification evidence became inaccessible, interrupting development and independent acceptance
- External Library backups survived and matched their recorded SHA-256 hashes
- Those backups allowed recovery of an earlier accepted repository baseline and a later in-progress source snapshot
- Source changes and receipts created after the latest saved snapshot have not been recovered from the currently accessible workspace or available backup chain
- Some lost evidence will require genuine re-execution; remembered results cannot replace missing acceptance receipts
- The assistant also allowed newer changes to accumulate locally while waiting for a verified checkpoint. That backup gap increased the recovery cost, but does not explain the environment transition
After I requested investigation before further recovery, the recovery job already in flight finished in a new directory. No coding, builds or tests have resumed.
Expected behavior
OpenAI’s guide says the cloud computer “can keep its state between periods of use”: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/dots/computers-and-apps
I understand that this wording does not define a complete durability guarantee. However, an ongoing development task needs a clear persistence contract: which paths survive, what events can replace state, how recent a restored snapshot should be, and how users are warned when work is at risk.
An unexpected transition should preserve recoverable work or clearly report what happened and how to retrieve the previous state.
Reproduction status
There is no deterministic reproduction. We have not deliberately rebooted, reset or filled the filesystem to reproduce this issue. The observed sequence was active work → stalled filesystem calls → execution disconnect → renewed access with recent files missing and older files present.

Requested investigation
1. Correlate this dot and execution session with the environment and storage history during approximately 02:35–03:01 UTC on October 10
2. Identify what caused the filesystem stalls and subsequent execution-service disconnect
3. Determine whether the task was attached to a replacement environment, an older snapshot, a different writable layer or another storage association
4. Preserve and locate the preceding writable layer and any newer snapshots before cleanup makes recovery harder
5. Confirm whether the missing source changes and evidence can be recovered
6. Explain the supported persistence guarantees for task scratch and shared workspace directories
7. Explain low-disk-space behavior, including whether it can trigger replacement or restoration and what warnings or recovery mechanisms exist
8. Clarify exactly what Pause and Reboot affect, including delegated tasks, active processes, filesystem state and snapshots
9. Correlate the earlier reported loss in this same dot conversation without assuming a common cause
10. Provide a supported method for durable, automatic checkpoints outside the execution filesystem
Privacy
This public draft omits account details, private project contents, full private paths, conversation/session identifiers and exact environment identifiers. Relevant correlation details and available diagnostic hashes can be supplied through an appropriate private support channel.
Current conclusion
Recent working state is demonstrably missing from the accessible environment, and the observed filesystem identity differs from an earlier verified record. The underlying cause and recoverability of the previous storage remain unresolved. Please investigate before treating this as an ordinary task interruption or user-initiated reset.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

No deterministic reproduction is available. The observed sequence was:
1. Continue an existing development task on the dot’s cloud computer, with source worktrees, Git history, test evidence and external Library checkpoints
2. Start an offline test against a pinned source revision at 02:24:37 UTC on October 10, 2026
3. Observe filesystem operations stall around 02:35, including independent file inspection and directory listing
4. Receive execution-service transport disconnection and recovery-timeout errors around 02:58
5. When commands work again around 03:01, inspect the original workspace paths
6. Find recent source and verification directories absent, older files still present, and reported filesystem usage reduced from approximately 30 GB to 3.3 GB
7. Compare diagnostics: the current overlay identifier differs from an earlier hash-verified environment record
I did not click Pause, Reboot, Delete or Reset. We have not deliberately reproduced the incident through rebooting or filling the disk. Available storage was low before the failure, but causation is unproven. The interrupted test’s final outcome is unknown. Private session identifiers can be supplied to support; token and context-window usage were not captured.

### What is the expected behavior?

Previously saved project files should remain accessible within the cloud computer’s supported persistence scope. If the platform replaces an environment or restores a snapshot, it should preserve recoverable work, disclose the transition and snapshot age, and provide recovery guidance.
Please clarify which directories persist, what events can discard or replace their state, and what happens when disk space becomes low. A running development task should not silently return to an older accessible state without a clear warning or recovery path.

### Additional information

This is a recurring user-visible issue in the same dot conversation. An earlier incident involved missing research progress described as 12–14 cycles/runs and led to explicit requests for frequent ZIP and laptop backups. Its exact cause and timing are not established here.
External Library backups survived this incident and were hash-verified. They recovered an accepted baseline and later in-progress work. Four subsequent repair areas, including eleven focused tests and later local-only verification records, remain absent from the recovered source/evidence set. Build caches and generated artifacts account for part of the disk-usage difference; we are not claiming 26 GB of unique source was permanently deleted.
Please preserve and investigate the preceding writable layer and snapshots, correlate environment/storage transitions during October 10, 02:35–03:01 UTC, and establish whether newer work is recoverable. Exact identifiers can be provided privately. No backend root cause has been established.
